prompt: `if (cents >= amount) { cents -= amount; }` on several threads is which kind of race?

choices.text: Check-then-act
choices.why: Right, with a read-modify-write inside it.

choices.text: Unsafe publication of the account
choices.why: The account was published by `start`; the race is in `withdraw`.

choices.text: A deadlock between the two tills
choices.why: Nothing waits for anything; the tills both act.

choices.text: A visibility problem that `volatile` would fix
choices.why: Both steps must happen together; `volatile` does not do that.

prompt: Why does `Overdraft.java` put `Thread.yield()` between the check and the subtraction?

choices.text: Because `yield` makes the check atomic
choices.why: It does the opposite.

choices.text: Without it the code would be correct
choices.why: The gap exists either way.

choices.text: To widen the gap so the failure shows on a quiet machine
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: To give the other tills a fair turn at the money
choices.why: It invites a switch exactly where switching is harmful.

prompt: `Counter.increment()` is `synchronized` and `get()` is not. What can go wrong?
hint: Every access goes through the same lock.

choices.text: Nothing: reads never need a lock
choices.why: A read needs the edge the lock creates.

choices.text: Increments may be lost again
choices.why: Increments still exclude each other.

choices.text: `get()` may return a stale value
choices.why: Right: no happens-before with the writers.

choices.text: The class will not compile with mixed methods
choices.why: It compiles.

prompt: Which of these follow the section's rules of thumb? Choose all that apply.
hint: Same lock, short block, a lock you own.

choices.why: No: everyone waits for the service.

choices.text: Locking writes on one object and reads on another
choices.why: No: two locks protect nothing.

choices.text: A `private final Object lock` used for every access
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Putting the check and the act in one block

prompt: A thread that holds a lock can enter another block on the same lock without waiting, because `synchronized` is ___.
Why must `unlock()` go in a `finally` block?

choices.text: An exception would otherwise leave it held forever
choices.why: Right: only `unlock()` releases it.

choices.text: Because `ReentrantLock` throws if it is unlocked twice
choices.why: That is true, and not the reason.

choices.text: `finally` runs on a separate thread
choices.why: It runs on the same thread.

choices.text: The compiler requires it
choices.why: It compiles without one.

prompt: What does a deadlocked Java program look like from outside?

choices.text: It stops, silently, forever
choices.why: Right; a thread dump finds it.

choices.text: It exits with status 1
choices.why: It never exits.

choices.text: It uses every processor at 100%
choices.why: Blocked threads use no processor.

choices.text: It throws `DeadlockException`
choices.why: No such exception is thrown; nothing is thrown.

prompt: Which change to `transfer` prevents the deadlock?

choices.text: Marking both accounts' fields `volatile`
choices.why: Visibility does not break a cycle of locks.

choices.text: Locking the two accounts in id order
choices.why: Right: one global order, no cycle.

choices.text: A longer `pause` between the two locks
choices.why: That makes the deadlock more likely.

choices.text: Locking `to` first and `from` second
choices.why: Still two orders, just swapped.
